input:
Start-up

Before any pressure is admitted, it is essential to confirm that the relief valve fitted is the valve called for on the line list, installed with its inlet connected to the protected system and its discharge connected to the discharge line. The direction of flow marked on the valve body is read and checked against the run of the pipework. The inlet and discharge block valves are then opened fully and left secured open, in whatever manner the plant uses for valves that must not be closed in service. A relief valve with a closed block valve on either side protects nothing at all, and no start-up should proceed while either valve remains shut.

The discharge path must be proved clear first. The drain at the low point of the discharge line is opened, the line confirmed to be running free, and the drain closed again. The outlet is confirmed to discharge to its safe location, with the area around it clear of people and temporary equipment. A pressure gauge is fitted at the valve inlet, or the gauge already there is proved, and confirmed to read zero with the system depressurised and to be readable from the operating position.

The operator inspects the valve and its joints, looking for damage in transit or during fitting, for corrosion on the body and the discharge flange, for missing or slack bolts at the joints, and for the maker's cap or seal still in place on the adjusting screw. No gag, blank or clamp is to be fitted to the valve; a gagged valve is effectively a removed valve and is reported as such. Any shipping restraint found is removed.

Pressure is then admitted slowly, raised by the normal start-up route in stages, with the inlet gauge watched as it rises. At each stage the rise is stopped and the joints are walked: a leak at either flange is made good before the pressure is raised further. As the system approaches normal operating pressure, the operator listens at the valve. A valve that simmers or leaks at the seat below its set pressure is reported in the log; the start-up may continue only where the leak is small and the discharge side stays dry, and the valve is then entered for inspection at the next opportunity. At normal operating pressure the inlet reading is recorded in the log, the valve is recorded as in service, and the system is handed over to normal operation.

Normal operation

In normal operation the relief valve stays shut while the pressure in the protected system remains within its normal operating band. The valve opens when the pressure reaches its set pressure and reseats once the pressure has fallen again; between such events it performs no work and requires no handling. The valve is not operated by hand in service, and is never used to control pressure: pressure control belongs to the normal control route of the system, and the valve is protection against the failure of that route.

The inlet pressure gauge is read on each round and the reading entered in the log. A reading trending upward across a shift is reported to the supervisor while the pressure is still inside the normal band; the valve is not the instrument that reports such a trend, and to wait for the valve to lift is to wait too long. Each reading is compared with the normal band, and a gauge that disagrees with the system instruments is changed, with the disagreement recorded.

The valve itself is inspected on the same round. The operator looks for leakage at the body joints and the bonnet, and checks the discharge line downstream: a discharge line that is warm although the system has not lifted the valve, or a hiss at the valve outlet, indicates a valve passing at the seat. Any such sign is noted in the log with the inlet pressure at the time. The operator also confirms that both block valves are still fully open and secured, that the discharge path remains unobstructed, and that nothing has been stored against the valve or under the outlet.

The setting of the valve is not to be touched: spring, adjusting screw and every other part are left alone, and a gag is never fitted to stop a passing valve. Adjustment and internal repair are workshop activities, carried out with the valve removed under the shutdown procedure and tested before it returns. Corrosion, mechanical damage, a broken seal on the adjusting screw, or a valve known to have lifted is reported to the supervisor and entered in the log on the shift on which it is found. After any lift, the operator confirms that the valve has reseated, the discharge line is clear and dry at its drain, and the inlet pressure is back within the normal band; the lift, the recovery pressure, and the state of the valve are recorded in the log.

Alarms

High inlet pressure. This alarm shows that the pressure in the protected system has risen above its normal operating band and is moving toward the set pressure of the valve. The alarm is acknowledged and the inlet gauge at the valve read to confirm the system reading. The pressure is reduced by the normal operating means: the inflow to the protected system is cut, and any heating input is reduced through its normal control route. Throughout, both block valves of the relief valve are kept fully open; no action under this alarm closes a valve between the protected system and its relief valve. If the pressure still rises and the valve lifts, the valve is allowed to discharge: the operator stands clear of the outlet, keeps other people clear, and continues cutting the inflow until the pressure falls and the valve reseats. The alarm, the highest pressure reached, and the action taken are reported to the supervisor and entered in the log. A system that has lifted its relief valve is not returned to full operation until the cause of the rise has been found.

Relief valve discharging. This alarm shows flow in the discharge line, or a high temperature in the discharge line at the valve outlet, and means the valve is open or passing. The first step is to read the inlet pressure gauge. Where the inlet pressure stands at or above the set pressure, the event is treated under the high inlet pressure alarm and the inflow is cut. Where the inlet pressure stands inside the normal operating band, the valve is passing at its seat: it is left in service, neither block valve is closed while the system remains pressurised, and the valve is not gagged. The supervisor and the maintenance group are notified, and the alarm entered in the log with the inlet pressure and the state of the discharge line. Both are monitored for the rest of the shift, and a valve that begins to pass more heavily is reported again at once. The valve stays as the protection of the system until the system can be shut down, and its repair is planned for that shutdown.

Shutdown

The protected system is taken out of service by its normal route and the pressure allowed to fall. The inflow is cut, any heating input stopped, and the system vented through its normal vent path until the inlet gauge at the valve reads zero. The zero is proved at the vent point of the section: a section still blowing at the vent is still pressurised, and the relief valve on such a section is not touched. Throughout the depressurisation the relief valve remains in service with both block valves open, as the protection of the system while pressure remains in it.

Only when the section has been proved depressurised are the inlet and discharge block valves closed. The pipework between the block valves and the valve is drained through the low-point drain, and the trapped section vented at its high point until drain and vent run dry and quiet. The valve and its short pipe runs are now isolated and depressurised, and only in this state is the valve unbolted. It is removed under the permit arrangements for the work, its weight supported as the last bolts come out, and blanks are fitted to the open flanges before the work party leaves the area. The removal, the reason for it, and the state in which the valve left the site are entered in the log. The protected system is not returned to service without a tested relief valve fitted and the start-up section of this chapter carried out on it.

Stop at each stage and walk the joints: a leak at either flange is made good before the pressure is raised further. Listen at the valve as the system approaches the normal operating pressure. A valve that simmers or leaks at the seat below its set pressure is reported in the log; the start-up continues only where the leak is small and the valve still holds the discharge side dry, and the valve is entered for inspection at the next opportunity. Normal operation

The relief valve stays shut while the pressure in the protected system stays within its normal operating band. The valve opens when the pressure reaches its set pressure and reseats when the pressure has fallen again; between those events it does no work and requires no handling. Do not operate the valve by hand in service, and do not use it to control pressure: control belongs to the normal control route of the system, and the valve is protection against the failure of that route.

Read the inlet pressure gauge on each round and enter the reading in the log. A reading that trends upward across a shift is reported to the supervisor while the pressure is still inside the normal band; the valve is not the instrument that reports the trend, and waiting for the valve to lift is waiting too long. Compare the reading with the normal band for the system each time; a gauge that disagrees with the system instruments is changed and the disagreement recorded.

Inspect the valve on the same round. Look for leakage at the body joints and at the bonnet, and check the discharge line downstream of the valve: a discharge line that is warm where the system has not lifted the valve, or a hiss at the valve outlet, shows a valve passing at the seat. Note the sign in the log with the inlet pressure at the time. Confirm that both block valves are still fully open and secured, that the discharge path is still unobstructed, and that nothing has been stored against the valve or under the outlet.

Keep hands off the setting: do not adjust the spring, the adjusting screw or any part of the valve, and do not fit a gag to stop a passing valve. Adjustment and internal repair are workshop work, done with the valve removed under the shutdown procedure and tested before it returns. Corrosion, mechanical damage, a broken seal on the adjusting screw, or a valve known to have lifted is reported to the supervisor and entered in the log on the shift on which it is found. After any lift, confirm that the valve has reseated, that the discharge line is clear and dry at its drain, and that the inlet pressure is back inside the normal band; record the lift, the pressure at which the system was recovered, and the state of the valve in the log.

Alarms

High inlet pressure. The alarm shows that the pressure in the protected system has risen above its normal operating band and is moving toward the set pressure of the valve. Acknowledge the alarm and read the inlet pressure gauge at the valve to confirm the system reading. Reduce the pressure by the normal operating means: cut the inflow to the protected system, and reduce any heating input by its normal control route. Keep the inlet and discharge block valves of the relief valve fully open throughout; no action under this alarm closes a valve between the protected system and its relief valve. If the pressure continues to rise and the valve lifts, let the valve discharge: stand clear of the discharge outlet, keep other people clear, and continue to cut the inflow until the pressure falls and the valve reseats. Report the alarm, the highest pressure reached, and the action taken to the supervisor, and enter the event in the log. A system that has lifted its relief valve is not returned to full operation until the cause of the rise has been found.

Relief valve discharging. The alarm shows flow in the discharge line, or a high temperature in the discharge line at the valve outlet, and it means the valve is open or passing. Read the inlet pressure gauge first. Where the inlet pressure stands at or above the set pressure, treat the event under the high inlet pressure alarm and cut the inflow to the system. Where the inlet pressure stands inside the normal operating band, the valve is passing at its seat: leave the valve in service, do not close either block valve while the system is pressurised, and do not gag the valve. Notify the supervisor and the maintenance group, and enter the alarm in the log with the inlet pressure and the state of the discharge line. Monitor both for the rest of the shift; a valve that begins to pass more heavily is reported again at once. The valve stays as the protection of the system until the system can be shut down, and its repair is planned for that shutdown.

Shutdown

Take the protected system out of service by its normal route and let the pressure fall. Cut the inflow, stop any heating input, and vent the system through its normal vent path until the inlet pressure gauge at the valve reads zero. Prove the zero at the vent point of the section: a section that still blows at the vent is still pressurised, and the relief valve on that section is not touched. The relief valve remains in service, with both block valves open, for the whole of the depressurisation; it is the protection of the system while pressure remains in it.

Close the inlet and discharge block valves only when the section is proved depressurised. Drain the pipework between the block valves and the valve through the low-point drain, and vent the trapped section at its high point until both drain and vent run dry and quiet. The valve and its short pipe runs are now isolated and depressurised, and only in that state is the valve unbolted. Remove the valve under the permit arrangements for the work, support its weight as the last bolts come out, and fit blanks to the open flanges of the inlet and discharge pipework before the work party leaves the area. Enter the removal, the reason for it, and the state in which the valve left the site in the log. The protected system does not return to service without a tested relief valve fitted and the start-up section of this chapter carried out on it.
